title: Hemingway’s lost generation turns 100
gist: Katherine Pangonis revisits Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises' at its centenary in Pamplona, arguing the novel's stripped-down style was radical in 1926 and its observations of social hierarchy endure, even though its antisemitism, homophobia and treatment of women make it a period piece. She also notes how the book turned San Fermín and Left Bank Paris into mass-tourism commodities while bullfighting attendance declines.

insights.claim: Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises', published by Scribner's in October 1926 when he was 27, was radical for its stripped-bare sentences and screenplay-like dialogue, and was an instant hit.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Cultural innovations that later become clichés were disruptive at launch; durable IP is built on stylistic breaks.
insights.quote: The novel was an instant hit.
insights.locator: The sentences are stripped almost bare.

insights.claim: Pangonis argues that novels survive their centenaries only if they can bear the weight of criticism from successive ages, and that Hemingway's observations of people and social hierarchies have aged well even though his values have not.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: A lens on long-lived cultural assets: durability comes from insight that survives shifting moral norms.
insights.quote: The novels that survive their centenaries are those capable of bearing the weight of the criticism of the next age, and the one beyond that.
insights.locator: Love him or hate him, Hemingway

insights.claim: Hemingway's 'iceberg' technique, described in Death in the Afternoon, holds that seven eighths of a story's meaning is concealed below the surface, which the author says explains why the novel rewards repeated re-reading.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Re-readability underpins the long tail value of literary catalogues.
insights.locator: There was so much I missed

themes.theme: Roman à clef and reputational damage

insights.claim: Hemingway based the novel's characters on real friends such as Lady Duff Twysden, Pat Guthrie and Harold Loeb with flimsy pseudonyms, and invented some of the most damaging incidents, ruining several reputations.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Thinly fictionalised accounts of real people carry lasting reputational and legal risk.
insights.quote: Sun was never without controversy. It ruined several lives, or at least reputations.

insights.claim: Hemingway ceded all rights and royalties for 'The Sun Also Rises' to his first wife Hadley as part of their divorce.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: An anecdote on how literary royalty streams are treated as divisible assets.

insights.claim: An early draft opened with 'This is a novel about a lady' and gave Brett's history, but the first chapter and a half was cut late on F. Scott Fitzgerald's advice, so Brett was originally intended as the main character.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Editorial decisions can reshape how a work and its creator are judged for a century.
insights.quote: This is a novel about a lady,

themes.theme: Moral reassessment of a canonical text

insights.claim: Pangonis calls 'The Sun Also Rises' an antisemitic text, citing the repeated derision of Robert Cohn's Jewishness, and also notes racism and a snide homophobia, arguing it should be read as a period piece.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Shifting social norms continually re-price the reputations of canonical cultural figures.

insights.claim: On re-reading, the author argues that Robert Cohn, whom narrator Jake invites readers to despise, looks like the novel's only honest sufferer.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Illustrates how re-reading with modern values inverts traditional interpretations.
insights.quote: begins, on re-reading, to look like the novel’s only honest sufferer.

insights.claim: San Fermín in Pamplona, which Hemingway introduced to much of the anglophone world as a secret, now draws hundreds of thousands of tourists, many of whom come because of a novel they have not read.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Literary works can create durable tourism demand that outlives actual readership.
insights.quote: now draws hundreds of thousands of tourists – many of whom come because of a novel they have not read.
insights.locator: The expatriate Paris of the Left Bank

insights.claim: Expatriate Left Bank Paris has become a walking tour with laminated maps, and its cafés now charge handsomely for their literary association.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Heritage association is monetised as a price premium in hospitality.
insights.locator: The expatriate Paris of the Left Bank

insights.claim: Bullfighting attendance is falling and Catalonia has tried to ban bullfighting outright, reflecting a shift in public sentiment the author shares as an animal lover.
insights.speaker: Katherine Pangonis
insights.so_what: Secular decline in traditional spectacles driven by animal-welfare values.
insights.quote: attendance is falling, Catalonia has even tried to ban bullfighting outright.
